summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on prefix/KV cache hit rates and prompt reuse strategy. Customer saw modest KV hit improvement after normalization; discussion covered canonicalization, TTL tradeoffs, deduping prompts, and next benchmark steps.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Nguyen (Redwood CSM), Priya Rao (ClarionHealth ML), Mike Lawson (ClarionHealth SRE), Daniel Cho (Product), Nora (Compliance)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick check the agenda is caching hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, and the next benchmark run. Sound good?
[00:18] Priya: Yep that works. We're mainly interested in two things: can we get stable improvement in end-to-end latency and drop token cost, and second, how much of our traffic can be covered by prefix/KV caching without breaking correctness.
[00:32] Samir (SE): Great. Quick recap from last week: we rolled out prefix normalization and enabled KV cache on the dev cluster. Initial numbers were: prefix cache hit rate around 27% and KV cache hit around 62% on the synthetic tests. Those numbers came from the demo harness I pushed to the bucket.
[00:50] Mike: When you say prefix cache, just to be clear, that's the prefix matching that looks for identical opening tokens and returns cached KV state?
[00:58] Samir: Yeah exactly. It's not full-context dedupe, it's basically canonicalized prefix matching + KV reuse. Note transcription sometimes shows K V cache but it's the same.
[01:12] Daniel: Were those synthetic tests matching our real traffic shape? We saw more prompt variability in prod.
[01:20] Samir: Good point. The synthetic harness was modeled on your sample but not the 48h production sample we requested. Priya?
[01:27] Priya: Right, we couldn't share the full sample yet, so test fidelity was medium. We did a quick run with 10k requests that favored templated prompts and that bumped prefix hits to ~45% in that run.
[01:42] Alex: OK so observed behaviour: with strict canonicalization (whitespace normalize, remove tracking tokens, lowercase where safe), prefix hit improves a lot on templated prompts, but we also saw a few false positives where the template had slot values that change final output meaning.
[02:00] Priya: That's our worry — for clinical triage prompts, small slots change the outcome. We need a safe strategy to reuse prefixes without leaking or changing downstream decisions.
[02:12] Samir: Suggested approach: 1) define canonicalization rules per route, 2) use prompt hashing with a whitelist of mutable slots, 3) set conservative TTLs so the KV cache doesn't serve stale completions for dynamic contexts. In our trial we used TTL=30s which still had some stale combo issues; lowering to 10s reduced risk and kept hit rate decent.
[02:41] Mike: Can you quantify 'decent'?
[02:43] Samir: On the templated test run: TTL 30s -> KV hit 62%, prefix hit 45%, end-to-end p50 latency 230ms. TTL 10s -> KV hit 58%, prefix hit 42%, p50 latency 250ms. The tradeoff is small latency bump for safer freshness. Those numbers are approximate — see the spreadsheet.
[03:05] Priya: That p50 is better than our baseline, but how about tail latency? Our SREs care about p95.
[03:12] Samir: p95 with TTL 10s was about 620ms in the test harness; with 30s TTL p95 dropped to 560ms because more caching reduced work, but again freshness risk. We also tested dedicated pinned model variants which gave lower variance.
[03:29] Alex: Important product note: Redwood supports routing policy so if a request hits a disallowed template we can route to dedicated pool or fall back model. That reduces correctness risk but costs more.
[03:40] Daniel: Routing to Dedicated pool — that would increase cost materially, right?
[03:43] Alex: Yes, dedicated inference is more predictable but unit cost is higher. It's an option for the small percentage of high-risk prompts.
[03:49] Nora (Compliance): On the compliance side we need an audit trail showing when cached responses were served vs generated live. Do you provide that?
[03:58] Jules (CSM): Yes, we capture trace logs per request and can flag cache-served responses. We'll share the log schema and sample audit extract. Action: I will send the SOC2 summary and log schema.
[04:08] Priya: Good. Back to prompt reuse — we want a lightweight approach that doesn't require rewriting all prompts. Any recommended quick wins?
[04:16] Samir: Three quick wins: 1) prefix canonicalization rules (trim session ids, normalize dates), 2) group similar routes and apply route-specific TTLs, 3) encourage prompt templates with clear slot delimiters so hashing works. Also dedupe client-side where you can — if the front-end can detect exact duplicate prompts in short windows, skip the call.
[04:36] Mike: About dedupe client-side — we have an edge cache and can plug in a quick hash check before hitting Redwood API, that'll help a lot.
[04:43] Priya: We tried client-side hashing earlier and it prevented some calls but introduced complexity on error handling. Would like Redwood to offer a sample lib.
[04:51] Samir: We have a small snippet in the repo, I'll attach link in the notes.
[04:56] Alex: Also we noticed tokenization differences across models can reduce prefix hit when you switch model variants. Recommendation: pin model families for a route during POC runs or canonicalize at Unicode codepoint level.
[05:08] Daniel: How much did model switching impact hit rate?
[05:11] Samir: In our A/B runs switching from r-instruct-v1 to r-chat-compat there was ~6-8% hit drop due to different tokenization and system prompt differences. So for the POC keep model stable.
[05:24] Priya: Next benchmark: we want you to run with our 48h sample, and then run a 100k request test to estimate steady-state hit. Is that in scope?
[05:33] Alex: Yes. We proposed: Redwood runs the benchmark in dev with your sample, we run three TTL variants (5s, 10s, 30s) and provide CSV with per-route hit rates, latency percentiles, and cost delta. We'll also share the raw logs link.
[05:46] Priya: Timeline?
[05:47] Alex: If you share the traffic by 2026-08-01 we can run benchmarks and share results by 2026-08-04.
[05:55] Mike: One more SRE question — cache eviction policy and memory impact. What's the recommended size and evict policy?
[06:02] Samir: We use LRU by default, can configure TTL and max entries per model/route. For your workload we recommend starting with 1M entries per node and monitor evictions. We'll provide a runbook with sizing heuristics.
[06:16] Priya: Excellent. A couple of open risks: 1) prompts with PHI — we need strict KMS encryption and no retention in hosted logs; 2) template slot leakage — need more conservative whitelist.
[06:27] Jules: On data residency and PHI, your account is on Dedicated trial and we can enable additional retention controls; I'll coordinate with product security.
[06:35] Nora: Please share the data flow diagram and the KMS controls.
[06:38] Jules: Will do.
[06:40] Alex: Quick recap and explicit next steps: Alex share spreadsheet + runbook link; Samir push canonicalization config and re-run tests with TTL 10s and 5s; Priya provide 48h traffic sample; Jules share SOC2 and log schema; schedule follow up for 2026-08-11.
[06:58] Priya: Sounds good.
[07:00] Alex: Any last comments?
[07:03] Daniel: Just that if the cache hit stays in the 40-50% range we think this will meaningfully reduce monthly token spend.
[07:09] Samir: Yep, and we'll include cost deltas in the benchmark.
[07:12] Alex: Great thanks everyone! We'll follow up with the links.

References / Links mentioned:

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker misattribution and minor word swaps; numeric stats are rounded and should be verified against raw logs.
